posts.content_md:
Not sure, got to keep thinking about that. I would assume it takes more then the single layer at the glass surfact to change to get white. We need a varying degree of angles.

 I took a different approach. Now bear with me, I am mapping this out in paint as I think about it and write it down. I will post the illutration at the end. 

I found that most glass, including float glass has an index of refraction of about 1.5 and what I could find on gelatin was 1.25 and water is 1.33. With that being said, as the light goes through the glass first it bends toward then normal because of the higher index of refraction, then it goes through the gelatin which bends it away from the normal. The light from the object pretty much goes straight from the object. Now, flip the plate, emulsion facing reference. The light is bent when encountering the emulsion towards the normal, then bent even more when encontering the glass. Again the light from the object is dead on. Now if we compare the reference angle of both gelatins we will see that we have a near reference start angle for the emulsion facing the object and a more normalized angle for the emulsion facing the reference. So we start off with 56 Degree ref. In the object facing we have close to 56 degree. But in the ref facing we have maybe 54 degrees or so. 

Now what really strikes me, is first of all the fringe is lying oppositely for the two. In viewing the hologram as it should be viewed the glass first light angle runs from glass and toward the bottom of the hologram. The emulsion first runs from glass and up. See it?

Secondly, lets look at the object light. It has to bend toward normal then bend back to almost original angle for glass first, whereas emulsion first it just continues on the bend from the emulsion index of refraction.

So where am I going with this, not sure, but there may be something in there. :think: Something to do with the way the light has to go through the glass first to interfer in the emulsion with the emulsion facing reference. More so then looking at what happens to the reference light, it is the reference light after all.

posts.author: a_k
posts.content_md:
John, it might be a bit more involved than that as the refractive index of gelatin (1.55-1.25 - before/after exposure) is not necessarily constant throughout the thickness of the coating. Rallison proposes a gradient of the refractive index of the gelatin along the thickness of the coating. According to his proposal at the interface glass/gelatin the refractive index is high with low variations and the refractive index decreases while its variations get larger across the film.

[http://www.xmission.com/~ralcon/dcgprocess/p2.html](http://www.xmission.com/~ralcon/dcgprocess/p2.html) 

![Image](http://www.xmission.com/~ralcon/images/dcg/p2/pg18.gif)

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Is the chirp of the grating to give a broadband effect related to the fringe contrast? At the top of the emulsion, the reference beam dominates since it hasn't been attenuated by the coating, while the object light has been through the whole emulsion so it is at its dimmest. But at the bottom of the emulsion, where the reference beam has gone through all of the thickness, it is at its weakest while the object beam has just entered the coating and will be at its strongest.

It's similar thinking to the above, I don't know if this helps the understanding, but this question/problem has been around for a while!

posts.author: Sergio
posts.content_md: As the figure above indicate, the average index after developing is 1.4 now so you can compute a bulk index of ~1.4 to give a bandwidth of more than 60nm, the chirping is due development process and the damping (variable index modulation ) is due nonuniform illumination, it gives even more broader spectral bandwidth.
